title: The aesthetic experience of interior spaces with curvilinear boundaries and various space properties in immersive and desktop-based virtual environments
research_question:
RQ 1. What are the aesthetic experience dimensions associated with virtual environments (VEs) and curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties of interior spaces?
RQ 2. Is there a difference in aesthetic experience dimensions based on VEs of interior spaces?
RQ 3. Is there a difference in aesthetic experience dimensions based on curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties of interior spaces?
RQ 4. Does interaction between VEs and curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties affect the aesthetic experience dimensions of interior spaces?
RQ 5. Is there a difference in presence based on VEs of interior spaces?
RQ 6. Do aesthetic experience dimensions have an impact on the presence scores in VE?

participants.description: 60 university students (37 females, 23 males) aged 19 to 30 years, with intact color perception.
participants.recruitment: Voluntarily from ID. Bilkent University, participated in both experiments.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 32 unique 360-degree virtual environment (VE) visualizations of interior spaces. These VEs featured either horizontal or vertical curved boundaries and systematically manipulated four architectural properties: size (small/large), light (dim/bright), texture (longitudinal/lateral), and color (cool/warm). Presented via head-mounted display (IVE) or desktop computer (DTVE).

measures.instrument: 7-point Likert scale, based on Elver Boz et al. (2022) definition: 'How pleased, satisfied or relaxed one feels in an environment, how safe and coherent they think the environment looks, and how they would like to behave in this environment such as whether they would like to spend time or enjoy exploring.'
7-point Likert scale, based on Elver Boz et al. (2022) definition: 'How excited, frenzied, jittery or contended one feels in an environment.'
7-point Likert scale, based on Elver Boz et al. (2022) definition: 'How mysterious or complex an environment looks or how stimulated one feels in that environment.'
Presence Questionnaire (PQ) adapted from Paes (2019) and Usoh et al. (2000) (SUS - Slater-Usoh-Steed instrument), 10 items.

findings.antecedent: Virtual Environment type (Immersive Virtual Environment - IVE vs. Desktop-based Virtual Environment - DTVE)
findings.consequent: Familiarity (aesthetic experience dimension)
findings.mechanism: IVE may make participants feel closer and 'like home' due to lack of external interruption and ability to move around, leading to higher familiarity.
findings.quote: IVE (m=3.83, sd=0.11) was more familiar than DTVE (m=3.36, sd=0.11).

findings.antecedent: Virtual Environment type (Immersive Virtual Environment - IVE vs. Desktop-based Virtual Environment - DTVE)
findings.consequent: Excitement (aesthetic experience dimension)
findings.mechanism: Consistent with familiarity, more familiar stimuli may appear relatively more predictable, satisfying, and less complex, contributing to excitement.
findings.quote: IVE (m=3.75, sd=0.09) was found to be more exciting than DTVE (m=3.56, sd=0.09).

findings.antecedent: Virtual Environment type (Immersive Virtual Environment - IVE vs. Desktop-based Virtual Environment - DTVE)
findings.consequent: Fascination (aesthetic experience dimension)
findings.quote: The fascination dimension showed no main effect of VEs (F(1,59)=1.78, p=0.18)

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear boundary type (Horizontal boundaries vs. Vertical boundaries)
findings.consequent: Familiarity (aesthetic experience dimension)
findings.mechanism: Familiar things are perceptually salient qualities of the built environment that can be manipulated independently in architectural design strategies.
findings.quote: Horizontal boundaries (m=4.03, sd=0.10) were more familiar than vertical boundaries (m=3.15, sd=0.11).

findings.consequent: Excitement (aesthetic experience dimension)

findings.quote: Vertical boundaries (m=3.77, sd=0.10) were found to be more exciting than horizontal boundaries (m=3.55, sd=0.08).

findings.quote: Vertical boundaries (m=4.30, sd=0.11) were found to be more fascinating than horizontal boundaries (m=3.60, sd=0.10).

findings.consequent: Excitement (aesthetic experience dimension)

findings.consequent: Excitement (aesthetic experience dimension)
findings.quote: The horizontal curvilinear boundaries were found marginally significantly more exciting than the vertical curvilinear boundaries for the IVE (t(59)=-1.86, p=0.07)

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear boundary type (Horizontal vs. Vertical) in Desktop-based Virtual Environment (DTVE)
findings.consequent: Excitement (aesthetic experience dimension)
findings.quote: whereas the two boundary types did not significantly differ from each other in terms of excitement for the DTVE (t(59)=0.84, p=0.40).

findings.antecedent: Virtual Environment type (Immersive Virtual Environment - IVE vs. Desktop-based Virtual Environment - DTVE)
findings.consequent: Presence score
findings.mechanism: IVE provides a more immersive experience, allowing participants to experience places without external factors or interruption and move around, leading to a higher sense of presence.
findings.quote: In Figure 7, there is a significant difference between IVE and DTVE (t=10.97, df=59 p<0.0001).

findings.antecedent: Excitement dimension of aesthetic experience
findings.consequent: Presence score in Immersive Virtual Environment (IVE)
findings.mechanism: Excitement, characterized by feelings of being wideawake, excited, frenzied, jittery, or contended, is a common predictor of presence.
findings.quote: The excitement dimension (β=0.53, t=4.37, df=57, p<0.001) is the only predictor that explains 24.34% of the variance of the architectural variables in the presence score of model 1 in IVE.

findings.antecedent: Fascination dimension of aesthetic experience
findings.consequent: Presence score in Immersive Virtual Environment (IVE)
findings.quote: The fascination dimension (β=0.45, t= 2.69, df=56, p=0.009) is the only predictor that explains 8.35% of the variance of the architectural variables in the presence score of model 2 in IVE.

findings.antecedent: Excitement dimension of aesthetic experience
findings.consequent: Presence score in Desktop-based Virtual Environment (DTVE)
findings.mechanism: Excitement, characterized by feelings of being wideawake, excited, frenzied, jittery, or contended, is a common predictor of presence.
findings.quote: The excitement dimension (β=0.33, t=2.6, df=57, p=0.012) is the only predictor that explains 10.18% of the architectural variables' variance in the model's presence score, as seen in Table 1.

mechanisms: Immersive Virtual Environments (IVE) enhance feelings of familiarity and 'being at home' by reducing external distractions and allowing for greater physical movement, which contributes to a stronger sense of presence.
Familiar stimuli are perceived as more predictable, satisfying, and less complex, which can influence excitement levels.
Perceptually salient qualities of the built environment, such as familiar or unexpected elements, can be independently manipulated in architectural design to affect aesthetic experiences.
A holistic approach combining boundary types and space properties allows for 'fascination' to emerge through interaction with the perception of the built environment.
implementation_implications: Designers can manipulate architectural variables in existing spaces to influence aesthetic experiences, which is substantial for renovating the built environment.
Immersive Virtual Environments (IVE) are more comparable to real-world situations than desktop-based VEs (DTVE), making IVE more suitable for human behavioral studies.
Findings can help designers and researchers create more immersive and realistic virtual experiences.

tables.description: Hierarchical multiple regression on VE's and the presence score, showing beta weights, R, R², ΔR², ΔF, and df for different models in IVE and DTVE.
key_stats: IVE Model 1: Excitement β=0.53, t=4.37, df=57, p<0.001, R²=0.27
IVE Model 2: Fascination β=0.45, t=2.69, df=56, p=0.009, R²=0.35
DTVE Model 1: Excitement β=0.33, t=2.6, df=57, p=0.012, R²=0.15

tables.description: Item-based results showing correlations (r) and p-values between individual Presence Questionnaire (PQ) items and aesthetic experience dimensions (Familiarity, Excitement, Fascination) for both Horizontal Boundaries (HB) and Vertical Boundaries (VB) in IVE and DTVE.
key_stats: DTVE-HB Familiarity: PQ2 r=0.274, p=0.03; PQ8 r=0.262, p=0.04
DTVE-HB Fascination: PQ1 r=0.282, p=0.02; PQ3 r=0.273, p=0.03
DTVE-VB Excitement: PQ3 r=0.375, p=0.01; PQ5 r=0.339, p=0.008

limitations: The age range of participants was restricted to 19-30 years, limiting the comprehensive understanding of aesthetic experience in older age groups.

All participants were university students, which might have introduced bias due to similar educational opportunities and potentially challenging aesthetic experience assessment for certain age groups.
The study used only two intensity levels for each space property (size, light, texture, color), suggesting that future research could explore more levels of intensity for a nuanced understanding.
